# Universal index laws for subalgebras generated by two primitive idempotents over finite chain rings

## Finding

Let \(R\) be a finite commutative chain ring of length \(m\geq1\), with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m=(\pi)\), residue-field size \(q\), and \(|R|=q^m\). Sample independently and uniformly two primitive (rank-one) idempotents \(E,F\in M_2(R)\). Let \(\mathcal A(E,F)\) be their **unital \(R\)-subalgebra**, including all scalar matrices, and let \(D\in\{0,\ldots,2m\}\) be defined by

\[
[M_2(R):\mathcal A(E,F)]=q^D,
\]

where the index is an additive-group index. Set

\[
B_m(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}(q-1)q^{m-i-1}z^i+z^m.
\]

The complete labeled ordered-pair index census is

\[
\boxed{\sum_{E,F}z^{D(E,F)}=q^{2m-1}(q+1)\left[(q-2)(q-1)q^{2m-2}+2\bigl(B_m(z)^2-(q-1)^2q^{2m-2}\bigr)\right].}
\tag{1}
\]

Thus \(D\) has probability generating polynomial equal to the bracketed factor in (1), divided by \(q^{2m-1}(q+1)\). In particular, the probability of full matrix-algebra generation is the known finite-field value

\[
\Pr(D=0)=\frac{(q-2)(q-1)}{q(q+1)}.
\tag{2}
\]

The new index enumeration is finer than this generation event. For a fixed primitive idempotent \(E\), the distinct attainable unital \(R\)-subalgebras \(\mathcal A(E,F)\) number \((m+1)^2\) if \(q>2\), and \((m+1)^2-1\) if \(q=2\). Their inclusion poset consists of two chains of length \(m+1\) in product order, with the greatest element missing exactly when \(q=2\).

For fixed \(q\) as \(m\to\infty\), the variables \(D\) converge in total variation to a universal \(D_\infty\) with

\[
\Pr(D_\infty=0)=\frac{(q-2)(q-1)}{q(q+1)},\qquad
\Pr(D_\infty=d)=\frac{2(d+1)(q-1)^2}{(q+1)q^{d+1}}\quad(d\ge1).
\tag{3}
\]

More precisely, the finite and limiting probabilities coincide for every integer \(0\le d<m\), and

\[
 d_{\mathrm{TV}}(D,D_\infty)\le
 \frac{2((q-1)m+q)}{(q+1)q^m}.
\tag{4}
\]

Despite this tight limiting logarithmic index, the expected **index itself** grows quadratically in \(m\):

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E[q^D]=\frac{(q-2)(q-1)+2\bigl([m(q-1)+q]^2-(q-1)^2\bigr)}{q(q+1)}
\sim\frac{2(q-1)^2}{q(q+1)}m^2.}
\tag{5}
\]

The limiting mean logarithmic index is \(\mathbb E[D_\infty]=4q/(q^2-1)\). All formulas hold in equal and mixed characteristic, with no assumption that \(R\) is a quotient of the integers.

## Assumptions and scope

A finite commutative chain ring has ideals \(R\supset\pi R\supset\cdots\supset\pi^mR=0\); each successive quotient has \(q\) elements. Define \(\nu(x)=i\) when \(x\in\pi^iR\setminus\pi^{i+1}R\), and \(\nu(0)=m\). An idempotent is primitive here when its image is a free direct summand of rank one. A *unital \(R\)-subalgebra* means an \(R\)-submodule closed under multiplication and containing \(I_2\); this scalar convention is essential. Equations (1)–(5) count all ordered primitive-idempotent pairs, including coincident and complementary pairs. The exponent \(D\) measures additive index, not matrix rank.

## Proof

**Step 1: normal form and multiplicity of primitive idempotents.** Since a finite local ring is local, every rank-one direct summand of \(R^2\) has a free complement. Thus \(\mathrm{GL}_2(R)\) acts transitively on primitive idempotents. Fix \(E=e_{11}\). Every other primitive idempotent is uniquely

\[
 F=\begin{pmatrix}t&b\\c&1-t\end{pmatrix},\qquad bc=t(1-t),\quad t,b,c\in R.
\tag{6}
\]

Indeed all primitive idempotents have trace one by similarity; conversely (6) has trace one and determinant zero, hence is idempotent by Cayley–Hamilton. Reducing modulo \(\mathfrak m\) shows it is primitive. Directly counting image and complementary kernel lines gives \(q^{m-1}(q+1)\cdot q^m=q^{2m-1}(q+1)\) primitive idempotents. Conjugation transitivity permits counting the second factor at \(E=e_{11}\) and multiplying by this total.

**Step 2: the precise generated order.** Multiplying (6) by \(E\) and \(I-E\) isolates \(b e_{12}=EF(I-E)\) and \(c e_{21}=(I-E)FE\). Conversely (6) lies in their scalar and diagonal span. Hence

\[
\boxed{\mathcal A(E,F)=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&bx\\cy&d\end{pmatrix}:a,d,x,y\in R\right\}.}
\tag{7}
\]

The displayed set is closed under multiplication, since off-diagonal entries lie in the principal ideals \((b)\) and \((c)\); it contains the generators. Consequently its additive index is \(|R/(b)|\,|R/(c)|=q^{\nu(b)+\nu(c)}\), proving \(D=\nu(b)+\nu(c)\). The ideals \((b),(c)\) determine the subalgebra exactly, and inclusion reverses each valuation. A pair of valutions is realizable if and only if its count below is positive.

**Step 3: a two-root Hensel dichotomy.** If at least one of \(b,c\) is nonunit, then \(a=bc\in\mathfrak m\). The polynomial \(t(1-t)-a\) has the two distinct simple roots \(0,1\) modulo \(\mathfrak m\), with derivatives \(1,-1\) respectively. Each lifts uniquely through the finite ideal filtration. Thus there are exactly two \(t\) for each \((b,c)\) with at least one nonunit. If both \(b,c\) are units, then for each unit \(b\) and each \(t\) with \(t,1-t\) units there is exactly one \(c=t(1-t)/b\). There are \((q-2)q^{m-1}\) eligible \(t\) and \((q-1)q^{m-1}\) unit \(b\); this gives \((q-2)(q-1)q^{2m-2}\) choices. The number of \(b\) of valuation \(i\) is \(B_i=(q-1)q^{m-i-1}\) for \(0\le i<m\) and \(B_m=1\). Thus the fixed-\(E\) bivariate valuation census is

\[
 N_{0,0}=(q-2)(q-1)q^{2m-2},\qquad
 N_{i,j}=2B_i B_j\quad\text{when }i+j\ge1.
\tag{8}
\]

Summing (8) over \(i+j\) yields (1). Every positive-index valuation pair is realized; the unit-unit pair is realized exactly when \(q>2\). This proves the subalgebra-poset assertion and (2).

**Step 4: limiting logarithmic index.** Divide the fixed-\(E\) census by \(q^{2m-1}(q+1)\). For \(1\le d<m\), all \(d+1\) pairs \((i,j)\) summing to \(d\) are strictly below \(m\); (8) gives exactly the second formula in (3), independent of \(m\). Formula (2) is independent of \(m\) as well. The mass in the limiting tail from \(d=m\) is

\[
 \sum_{d=m}^{\infty}\frac{2(d+1)(q-1)^2}{(q+1)q^{d+1}}
 =\frac{2((q-1)m+q)}{(q+1)q^m}.
\]

The common coefficients below \(m\) imply that the finite distribution has precisely the same total tail mass; the total variation difference is therefore no greater than this common mass, proving (4) and normalization of (3). The stated limiting mean follows by differentiating the rational generating function

\[
\mathbb E[z^{D_\infty}]=\frac{(q-2)(q-1)}{q(q+1)}+
\frac{2(q-1)^2}{q(q+1)}\left[(1-z/q)^{-2}-1\right].
\]

**Step 5: critical expectation.** Evaluating (1) at \(z=q\) and using

\[
B_m(q)=q^{m-1}(m(q-1)+q),\qquad B_m(0)=(q-1)q^{m-1}
\]

produces (5). Its quadratic growth is compatible with weak and total-variation convergence of \(D\), because the unbounded function \(q^D\) is not uniformly integrable.

## Verification

The standalone Python file `checker.py` exhaustively enumerates all matrices (6) in nine finite chain rings, verifies matrix idempotence and the valuation-index histogram, and checks the predicted subalgebra as the linear span of \(I,E,F,EF,FE\) in selected small cases. Rings include \(\mathbb Z/2\), \(\mathbb Z/3\), \(\mathbb Z/5\), \(\mathbb Z/4\), \(\mathbb Z/9\), \(\mathbb Z/8\), \(\mathbb Z/27\), and dual-number rings \(\mathbb F_2[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)\), \(\mathbb F_3[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)\). Its replay output is included in `checker_output.txt`. These finite computations check boundary cases and both characteristic regimes; the proof establishes the universal assertions independently of enumeration.

## Relationship to prior work

Rowen and Segev [1] prove the general structural theorem for associative algebras generated by two idempotents, including the central parameter \((E-F)^2\), a matrix-algebra generation criterion, and the classical exceptional \(\mathbb F_2\) case. The simple full-generation threshold (2) therefore is **not presented as a new structural criterion**. Their results do not supply the labeled index-refined distribution (1), the valuation-pair order spectrum (8), or the limiting and critical-moment laws (3)–(5). Ito and Terwilliger [2] study the universal algebra of two systems of orthogonal idempotents over a field, rather than the index distribution of finite local-ring matrix suborders. The published finite-field all-arity generation census [3], inspected in full, proves the full-generation count (2) as a special case, but not the positive-index chain-ring strata. Another published complete field-only trace-orbit census [4] works with scalar-free ring generation rather than the unital coefficient-ring suborders considered here. The novelty assessment remains subject to possible unindexed equivalent enumeration.

## Limitations

The theorem is restricted to \(2\times2\) matrices, *primitive* idempotents, and finite **commutative chain rings**, with scalars included in the generated algebra. It does not determine the distribution of subalgebra conjugacy classes when both \(E,F\) vary, and it does not claim analogous universality over all local rings. Equation (2) is a known-type consequence, not a separate novelty claim. Full historical uniqueness and external independent validation have not been established.
